DELIVERY TARGET: 35 seconds.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
The project began with SalesMesh, where independent agents onboard customers beyond direct supervision. A document alone does not establish that the person presenting it is its owner or is live. Verity connects identity evidence to an enforceable access decision. The recorded hosted test illustrates why evidence quality matters: an unreadable card triggered recapture before the system made a decision.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

BACKGROUND
The project originated in the SalesMesh distributed-sales setting. Independent agents can act on behalf of a platform and interact with customers, so access should depend on identity evidence. The system is a browser-based implementation for agent registration and verification. It does not cover all customer KYC, transaction monitoring or post-onboarding behavioural fraud. Registration guardrails are separate from the SVM. Do not claim that the project measured reductions in time, staff workload or fraud loss.

Sources: Final report §§1.1, 1.4 and 1.5; Chapter 6.

PROBLEM
Frame the problem around the affected parties: platforms, administrators, agents and customers. A valid-looking document is insufficient without consistency and presence checks. The contribution is a coordinated, auditable workflow rather than a claim to detect every forged document or modern spoof. The report identifies these threats through literature and requirements analysis, not a measured local fraud-prevalence study.

Sources: Final report §§1.2, 2.3 and 2.6.

SIGNIFICANCE
The significance is the integration of verification evidence, recorded outcomes and platform access in the agent-onboarding context. Transparency here means inspectable inputs, model versions, provenance and audit records; an RBF SVM is not inherently a human-readable rule explanation. The project also reports where the model fails. In the revised evaluation, 157 of 1,200 cases labelled Manual Review or Rejected were classified as Verified. This is why the contribution includes measured limits and why human oversight remains necessary.

Sources: Final report §§1.4, 2.6, 5.6 and 6.2.6.

text:
DELIVERY TARGET: 25 seconds.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
The literature separates face matching from liveness and document consistency. Commercial services combine these checks, but their reviewed decision policies are proprietary. Verity’s contribution is an inspectable integration for agent onboarding: identity evidence becomes six scores, a recorded decision and controlled access, with administrator review for uncertain cases.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

LITERATURE AND GAP
This is a literature comparison, not a matched trial against commercial products. The report reviewed Advance.AI, SEON, Facia.AI, Joinble, VerifyID and Jumio. It identifies closed decision policies and the integration burden for this project context. ArcFace supports embedding-based matching. Liveness studies address a separate threat and highlight domain shift. The implemented OCR score measures agreement with registration details, not document tamper detection. Verity does not perform AML screening or prove document authenticity. The project response should be described as an integration and evaluation contribution, not an unsupported claim of universal novelty or commercial superiority.

Sources: Final report §§2.4–2.7 and Table 2.1; cited studies as listed in the report.

CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK
Inputs are document and facial evidence plus profile details. OpenCV performs quality checks before downstream processing and supplies raw blur, brightness and contrast. EasyOCR supplies identity-text agreement, ArcFace/InsightFace supplies face similarity and Silent-Face supplies liveness. The model combines all six scores, so similar face scores can produce different outcomes. The backend stores scores, the decision and its provenance, and links the result to access control. Manual Review is an explicit outcome requiring administrator handling. Duplicate identities, disposable email and attempt guardrails act independently of the SVM. Significant operations call the audit logger; source calls alone do not prove that every event persisted.

Sources: Final report §2.7, Figure 2.6 and §§5.3.3–5.3.4.

DELIVERY TARGET: 35 seconds.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
The browser sends identity evidence to Express, which checks authentication and coordinates the Flask AI service. Quality checks precede OCR, face matching and liveness. The classifier combines their scores, and the backend records the decision and access state in Supabase. I integrated pretrained image models and trained the decision SVM. The architecture separates image processing from application access control.

Release evidence: the report records v3.1.1 publication to GHCR on 19 November 2026 and matching saved/live version labels. The measured hosted run was v3.1.0. The recorded Azure allocation is not a measured minimum, training-time result or cost estimate.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

TECHNOLOGY
The stack separates presentation, application coordination, image processing and persistence. Face matching uses pretrained buffalo_l resources through InsightFace. MiniFASNet resources supply Silent-Face liveness scores. The browser MediaPipe challenge is separate from the server anti-spoofing model and is not camera attestation. Optional WebAuthn stores public-key credentials; it does not give Verity the device biometric template. Hosting is Vercel for the frontend, Render for the backend, Azure Container Apps for AI, and Supabase for authentication, PostgreSQL and Storage. GitHub Actions built the container and published it to GHCR. The report records 4 vCPU and 8 GiB for Azure, not measured minimum requirements, peak memory, training time or costs. Some image-library versions were unpinned.

Sources: Final report Tables 5.1–5.2 and §§5.2.1–5.2.3.

ARCHITECTURE
Trace a captured document and selfie from the browser to the Express API, then to the Flask quality, OCR, face, liveness and SVM endpoints. The backend validates tokens and roles and writes relational evidence and outcome records in Supabase. Supabase authentication also participates in sign-in; the diagram shows the main protected verification flow. Backend-to-AI requests use X-API-Key and HTTPS in the hosted setup. Storage uses a private bucket with signed viewing URLs, though deployed access settings were not comprehensively tested. The report records the v3.1.1 image publication on 19 November 2026 and a matching live/report version display, while the measured hosted run was earlier v3.1.0. Separate saved evaluation from observed deployment. Do not describe 4 vCPU/8 GiB as a benchmarked minimum or invent cost.

DELIVERY TARGET: 45 seconds.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
Development used Agile iterations and object-oriented analysis and design. For the model, stored measurements from LFW, NUAA and MIDV informed synthetic score distributions. Independent draws supplied seven thousand training cases, fifteen hundred development cases and three thousand final evaluation cases. Scaling used training data only. Version 3.1.1 is an RBF SVM with class weighting. Its learned decision is separate from the application’s threshold fallback when inference is unavailable.

FALLBACK REFERENCE
Reject if face < 50, liveness < 0.50, OCR < 0.40, or blur < 80 together with face < 65. Otherwise verify only if face > 80, liveness > 0.75 and OCR > 0.70. Remaining valid-score cases go to Manual Review. The basis is placeholder_threshold. Missing, malformed, non-finite or out-of-range inputs fail before fallback.

The 25–50 face-score region is an evaluation probe, not a hard runtime override. Training estimates LIBSVM class probabilities, and no online learning occurs.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

METHODOLOGY
The software process used Agile/Scrum and Object-Oriented Analysis and Design. The ML method reused stored measurements from 1,000 LFW face pairs, 1,200 NUAA presentations, and 500 MIDV quality frames with MIDV OCR measurements. These informed distributions, not real three-class KYC labels. Replay-Attack was not used. Version 3.1.1 generated 11,500 cases with independent seeds 120141, 120142 and 120143. Scaling was fitted only on the 7,000 training rows and then reused with clipping for development and test. Final evaluation cases were generated after selection. The original 1,500-case v3.1.0 test set was an additional comparison and is excluded from the 11,500 total. Pretrained image models were used as provided; the project trained the decision classifier.

Sources: Final report §§3.1–3.4, §§5.3.6–5.3.7 and Table 5.6.

SVM AND FALLBACK
The v3.1.1 model is a six-input LIBSVM RBF C-SVC trained on 7,000 cases with C=10 and gamma=1. Class weights are 7000/(3 × class count): Verified 0.7778, Review 0.9722 and Rejected 1.4583. LIBSVM probability estimation is fitted during training. No hand-assigned OCR weight or fixed 25–50 review override is used. The face probe band tests learned behaviour: with OCR and liveness fixed at 1.0 across three additional quality profiles, 74/75 cases were referred and one verified. The predecessor verified all 75. Missing, non-finite, wrongly typed or out-of-range inputs fail before prediction or fallback. The application fallback is labelled placeholder_threshold, and its 0/1 outputs are not calibrated probabilities. The 5000-ms source default applies separately to model-status and prediction requests, not the whole workflow. Classifier probabilities reflect the synthetic mixture. No online learning occurs.

Sources: Final report Table 5.5, §§5.3.5–5.3.7 and §5.4.3; backend/src/services/accessControlService.js; ai-service/ml/experiments/face_review/scaler.json.

text:
DELIVERY TARGET: 45 seconds.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
Version 3.1.1 reached 86.07 percent accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.8211 on the revised synthetic evaluation. Against the same cases, it improved on version 3.1.0, but performance fell on the original scenarios, showing the effect of changed labels. The other classifiers were close. The critical error is that 157 of 1,200 non-Verified labels received verification. These results support further controlled evaluation rather than a real-applicant accuracy claim.

PRESENTATION PRIORITY
Point to the headline result, the opposite direction on the original scenarios, and the incorrect approvals. Do not read each comparator row. The table is available for follow-up. The calibrated tree has nine additional correct predictions, with a paired 95% accuracy-difference interval from −0.50 to +1.10 percentage points. No clear superiority claim follows.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

EVALUATION
Headline evaluation: 2,582/3,000 correct, accuracy 0.8606667, macro F1 0.8211454 and weighted F1 0.8607976. Actual classes by row and predictions [Verified, Review, Rejected] by column: Verified [1668,116,16]; Review [132,419,49]; Rejected [25,80,495]. Class precision/recall/F1: Verified 0.9140/0.9267/0.9203; Review 0.6813/0.6983/0.6897; Rejected 0.8839/0.8250/0.8534. Incorrect approvals equal 132+25=157 of 1,200 non-Verified labels, 13.08%; among 1,825 predicted verifications they are 8.60%. The denominators differ. On revised cases v3.1.0 accuracy was 75.93%, macro F1 0.6708; v3.1.1 accuracy 86.07%, macro F1 0.8211. On original cases they were 76.73%/0.6794 versus 67.33%/0.6505. Original Verified-to-Review counts increased from 62/900 to 260/900. The additional model comparison is supplementary saved evidence beyond the final report’s earlier comparator discussion. It uses the same revised splits. The calibrated tree has nine more correct predictions, but its paired accuracy-difference 95% interval is −0.50 to +1.10 percentage points. Do not claim clear superiority. Predicted review counts: full SVM 615, identity SVM 615, tree 684, calibrated tree 599. Twenty-repeat permutation macro-F1 decreases: face 0.294426, liveness 0.153926, OCR 0.101878, blur 0.005161, contrast 0.003708, brightness 0.000780. These are aggregate sensitivities, not individual-decision percentage weights.

Sources: Final report §§5.4.3–5.4.4 and Tables 5.12–5.15; backend/src/data/model-evaluation-3.1.1.json; ai-service/ml/experiments/face_review/comparison_models.json and README.md.

DELIVERY TARGET: 15 seconds.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
I will now demonstrate one verification workflow, a recapture case and the resulting agent and administrator views. The figures below are dated evidence from the report, separate from today’s demonstration.

DEMONSTRATION BUDGET: 8 minutes.
0:00–0:45: introduce the signed-in agent and test case.
0:45–2:30: capture the ID and selfie, including the browser challenge.
2:30–3:45: show a prepared capture-quality error and recovery, or clearly labelled recorded evidence.
3:45–5:15: submit and inspect actual scores, decision basis, model version and access.
5:15–6:45: inspect the same request and audit trail in the administrator browser.
6:45–8:00: explain the outcome, acknowledge the evidence limit and return to slide 9.

Do not repeat the model table in the demo. If a delay consumes the buffer, move to labelled backup evidence instead of waiting indefinitely.

REHEARSAL AND SETUP
Use a tested build, a consenting test participant and the project’s approved sample evidence. Sign in before presenting. Keep an agent browser and a separate administrator browser ready, with passwords kept in a password manager. Verify the current deployment before the defence. If unavailable, use a tested local build or clearly label report evidence as recorded backup. This presentation does not claim a fresh deployment test was performed while authoring the slides.

SCENARIO: AGENT COMPLETES IDENTITY VERIFICATION
1. Open the agent workflow and explain the profile details being compared with the ID.
2. Capture or upload the document and complete live selfie capture, including the browser head-turn challenge. Show one safe capture-quality failure or recorded recapture example, then recover with suitable evidence. Do not promise that every deliberately poor input will trigger the same error.
3. Submit. Show the recorded scores, decision basis and model version. Explain OCR agreement, face match and liveness as separate evidence.
4. Show the resulting agent access state. If the actual result is Review or Rejected, explain it honestly rather than trying to force an approval.
5. In the administrator browser, inspect the same request, linked scores, evidence and audit trail. Demonstrate an administrator decision only in a prepared, authorised test case. The report’s hosted evidence did not exercise the manual-review or rejection branches, so distinguish implemented paths from previously observed results.
6. Open the model evaluation view and compare the two versions on the same revised 3,000 synthetic cases. Explain 86.07% accuracy, macro F1 0.8211 and the consequential false-approval count. The 157 errors have 1,200 non-Verified labels as their denominator.
7. State one operational limitation and the next validation step: independently labelled real applicants and representative capture/attack conditions.

BACKUP EVIDENCE
The recorded 5 November 2026 v3.1.0 case requested recapture for a card too small for OCR, then verified the second submission, granted access and retained twelve audit events. The 13.6-second interval is one observation, not a latency benchmark. Local 46/46 tests are dated 23 October 2026 and must not be described as a full v3.1.1 regression.



REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

SEQUENCE
The diagram separates user, application, AI and persistence responsibilities. The application orchestrates the quality, OCR, face and liveness calls, validates the six inputs, and obtains an SVM outcome. Quality failure stops downstream processing and requests another capture. Scores, requests, decisions and access records are separate entities. The administrator path is conditional: a review notification exposes the case, an authorised approval or rejection updates the outcome and access record, and the action is logged. The displayed sequence expresses the implemented design, not proof that all branches ran in a hosted test. The recorded hosted run exercised recapture and verification only. The application fallback is documented in the model-development notes.

Sources: Final report Figure 4.5 and §§5.3.3–5.3.5.

SYSTEM TESTING
The 46 tests include 6 SVM contract tests, 2 experiment tests, 4 improvement tests, 2 backend decision tests, 5 retention tests, 9 passkey service tests, 1 passkey route test, 1 database migration test and 16 frontend tests. They passed on 23 October 2026, before v3.1.1. The six SVM tests were rerun after v3.1.0; the full 46 were not rerun. Live exports contained 12 requests across eight agent identifiers, nine linked decisions, five svm_model and four placeholder_threshold bases, and three pending requests. No adjudicated identity labels or historical model-version fields were present. The hosted case on 5 November used v3.1.0. Second-attempt scores were face 64.13, live 0.9998, OCR 1.0, blur 87.79, brightness 156.90, contrast 52.56. The outcome was Verified, probabilities [0.842,0.134,0.024], with access and 12 audit events. The 13.6-second interval is a single observation, not average latency. Manual review, hosted rejection, admin intervention, concurrency, comprehensive security and participant usability were not established. These are historical records, separate from the current demonstration.

Sources: Final report §§5.4.1–5.4.2, Tables 5.8–5.11; documentation/final_draft_evidence.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
The source implements role checks, optional passkeys, private images and registration guardrails. Verified images have a three-business-day cleanup policy. The report also records unfinished work: consent handling, expiry for other images and metadata, and recovery verification. I therefore distinguish implemented controls from the remaining requirements and do not claim compliance certification.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

SECURITY AND RETENTION
Security evidence is bounded. Source implements token and role checks, optional WebAuthn, registration guardrails, server-side AI credentials and signed URLs. Uploads accept JPEG/PNG up to 5 MiB per file. Attempt guardrail defaults are three counted events in a 24-hour window; three strikes lead to rejection, with administrator reset. Retention code considers the latest verified request and expires image evidence after three Monday–Friday business days in Africa/Nairobi, without holiday exclusions. It removes objects and clears file references while retaining records. Five local mocked tests passed; live deletion scheduling was not demonstrated. Amended requirements for 30-day pending/review/rejected/abandoned images and 180-day metadata expiry are incomplete. Applicable consent, notice record, backend enforcement and withdrawal handling were not found. Daily Google Drive backups were reported, but restoration, protections and the seven-day design expiry were not verified. Production-origin separation and the CAPTCHA accessible alternative remain unverified. Legal processing basis, biometric safeguards and overseas-hosting review remain unresolved in the report. No legal-compliance conclusion follows from the architecture or from hosting.

Sources: Final report §§5.2.2–5.3.3, §§5.4.1–5.4.2 and §5.6.3; documentRetentionService.js.

SUGGESTED SPOKEN EXPLANATION
Verity delivers the core verification and access workflow and a reproducible model experiment. The development objective is achieved, while operational validation remains partial. The next priorities are completing the safeguards, evaluating independently labelled applicants and measuring administrator correction. Further model updates should remain controlled, versioned and supported by untouched evaluation data.

REFERENCE DETAIL — use only for follow-up questions, not as a script.

CONCLUSIONS
Close against the objectives. The project implemented and hosted the core workflow, combined pretrained image components with a trained SVM, preserved decision provenance and provided administrator handling. The synthetic findings are reproducible but do not establish real-applicant accuracy, fairness, attack resistance or operational readiness. The development objective is achieved for the core system; the full amended requirements and testing objective remain partial. The highest priorities are informed collection and retention, isolated recovery testing, origin and human-check controls, independent labelled validation, and measurement of administrator correction. Future model updates should use governed, independently checked labels, an untouched evaluation set and explicit error-cost and review-capacity criteria. Administrator decisions do not automatically become ground truth. Periodic retraining remains offline with versioning and rollback.

Sources: Final report Chapter 6, particularly §§6.2–6.4.
